description: GGUF images written by the Python interp exporters and loaded by the Rust runtime

constraints: weights, mu, and sigma share one 1-D width
layer is a 0-based decoder block index
N is 1-based: direction.N steers decoder block N, and block 0 is unsteerable
every direction tensor shares one width
at least one direction tensor is present

notes.layer_numbering: The two artifacts number layers differently, and the difference is deliberate. probe.layer is 0-based because it names the block whose post-block residual the probe scores. direction.N is 1-based because llama.cpp and repeng number control vectors that way. Both sides already enforce their own rule independently - export.py refuses min(directions) < 1, and cpu.rs refuses layer < 1 - which is exactly why the end-to-end check matters more than either guard alone.
notes.reader_ignores: ControlVector::from_gguf reads no metadata at all: it neither checks general.architecture nor uses model_hint or layer_count, and selects tensors purely by the direction. prefix. The two metadata keys are therefore writer-only in practice. A probe image passed as a control vector still fails, but on 'holds no direction.<layer> tensors' rather than on an architecture mismatch.
notes.comparison_is_semantic: The committed fixtures are compared by parsed content - architecture, metadata keys and values, tensor names, widths, and values - never byte for byte. gguf is pinned, but a version bump may legitimately change padding or alignment, and a byte comparison would report that as exporter drift.
notes.float_exactness: Fixture values are chosen to be exact in f32, so a round trip through the writer and the Rust parser is an equality comparison and needs no tolerance.
